per_ply.human_comment:
This move co
ntraddicts the strategical principles indicated by the theory. Since Turn knew
that Mikenas had a deep theoretical preparation, he decided this line of play
in order to surprise the opponent.

A bit inaccurate. The
following continuation would have lead to interesting complications: 6. Bd2
Bb7 7. Qg3 O-O 8. d5
per_ply.system_comment: The most accurate move, 6.Bd3, holds the balance (-0.11, Stockfish:16) along [pv:Bd3 Ba6 Ne2 d5 O-O], at the cost of a line that may leave White's back rank vulnerable—an exposed back rank often decides games once the center opens. Bd2 leads to equality as a comparable option via [pv:Bd2 Bb7 Qd1 O-O Nf3], where Black's back rank could come under similar pressure instead.

per_ply.human_comment:
White hoped in the reply 7. .. 0-0
8.Ne2 with initiative on the kingside after 9.e4.

In fact, the capture
8. Qxg7 after 8... Rg8 9. Qh6 Rxg2 would have given a very promising position
to Black.

An energetic reply, revealing Mikenas character in that
period: enthusiasm, courage and imagination. Which is the general strategy of
the young people: attack, and don't care about possible losses.

per_ply.system_comment: White's most accurate move, improving piece activity so the pieces are actively placed—active pieces tend to keep the opponent tied down. It leads to a slight advantage for Black (-0.40, Stockfish:16) along [pv:Nf3 gxf4 exf4 Rg8 Qf2], where the continuation may leave White with a hanging piece. Qh3 is a comparable option, likewise leading to a slight advantage for Black along [pv:Qh3 gxf4 Nf3 Qe7 exf4], though that path may leave Black's back rank vulnerable deeper in the line.

The most accurate move for Black, maintaining the advantage (-0.36, Stockfish:16) along [pv:Rg8 Qf2 Qe7 Bd2 Nb4], as the line may leave White with a hanging piece and weak targets to attack. Qe7 was a comparable option, leading to a slight advantage for Black [pv:Qe7 Bd2 Rg8 Qf2 Nb4], with the potential to target the bishop on d3, but Rg8 keeps Black's edge sharper and later feeds a rook onto the seventh rank.

per_ply.human_comment:
The right continuation even if comes from intuition
rather than calculation. The consequences of 11... Rxg2 12. Qxg2 Nxd4 13. Qg7
Nxf3+ 14. Kf2 were unclear. Not even convincing 11... Nh5 12. Bxh7

When problems are complex the right reply is not always found. Perhaps better
was 12. Qxd4 although even in this case Black can keep some more possibilites
in view of the endgame. For example: 12... Bc5 13. Qe5 Rxg2 14. Ne4 Bxe4 15.
Bxe4 Ng4 16. Qh8+ Ke7 17. Qxd8+ Rxd8 18. Ne5 Bb4+ 19. Kf1 Rf2+ 20. Kg1 Re2 and
the position and the pawns are an adequate compensation for the sacrificed
material.
per_ply.system_comment: White missed the chance to target the bishop on d6 and the potential to strip Black of the bishop-pair advantage—often a lasting edge when lines open. Instead, 12.Nxd4 concedes a slight advantage to Black (+0.00 → -0.52, Stockfish:16) along [pv:Nxd4 Rxg2 Qf1 Ng4 Be4]: the king is now safe, and the recapture may eventually set up pressure on the bishop on b7. Black's...Rxg2 in the line plants a rook on the seventh and keeps the initiative. Qxd4 leads to equality along [pv:Qxd4 Rxg2 Ne4 Bxe4 Bxe4].

Black's most accurate move, maintaining the advantage (-0.53, Stockfish:16) along [pv:Rxg2 Qf1 Ng4 Be4 Qh4+], placing a rook on the seventh rank—a post that is notoriously hard to dislodge and keeps lasting pressure on the enemy camp. Bc5 is a comparable alternative that leads to equality via [pv:Bc5 Bf1 Ng4 Qd2 Qf6], targeting the knight on d4 and setting up lines where White may leave a piece hanging, but Rxg2 preserves more of Black's edge.

White's most accurate move, keeping Black's edge to a slight advantage (-0.47, Stockfish:16) after [pv:Qf1 Ng4 Be4 Qh4+ Kd1], whereas a slip on the next turn would let that edge grow sharply. Qxg2 was clearly weaker, giving Black a winning advantage [pv:Qxg2 Bxg2 Rg1 Bb7 Be3], even though that capture would immediately have left the white king safer and could have made the rooks more active on the open files deeper in the line.

per_ply.human_comment:
A serious mistake would have been 13... Ng4
for 14. Be4 Qh4+ 15.Kd1 Nf2+ 16. Kc2 and the attack vanishes.

Again an inaccurate move which will cost material. 14. Nce2 was relatively
better but after 14... Ng4 Black's attack would be irresistible.
per_ply.system_comment: Nf3 concedes a winning advantage to Black (-0.22 → -1.95, Stockfish:16), as Rf2 punishes it along [pv:Nf3 Rf2 Qxf2 Bxf2+ Kxf2], forcing a queen trade on f2 and a king recapture that leaves White worse off. White missed the chance to lead to equality with Rg1 [pv:Rg1 Rxh2 Be3 Rxb2 O-O-O], which would have activated the rooks on the open files—where they exert the most pressure—and improved the pawn structure.

The most accurate move, maintaining Black's advantage (-2.21, Stockfish:16) through [pv:Rf2 Qxf2 Bxf2+ Kxf2 Ng4+], as it leaves White with a hanging piece — loose material often becomes a decisive target. In return, Black's pieces are more passive, yet the follow-up may push White's king toward g3. Rg7 was clearly weaker, leading to a slight advantage for White after [pv:Rg7 Bd2 Ng4 Qe2 Nf2], where Black could only have targeted the rook on h1 deeper in the line.

This move gives Black a winning advantage (-2.17, Stockfish:16), and after [pv:Qxf2 Bxf2+ Kxf2 Ng4+ Kg3] White's king is pushed from f2 toward g3. Be2 is clearly weaker—it also gives Black a winning advantage via [pv:Be2 Rxf1+ Rxf1 d5 cxd5], where White's king would be safer and the pawn structure may improve further on, easing doubled, isolated, and backward pawn problems—but Qxf2 remains White's best try.

15...Bxf2+ is the most accurate move, maintaining Black's advantage (-2.29, Stockfish:16) through [pv:Bxf2+ Kxf2 Ng4+ Kg3 Bxf3], where White's king may come under pressure—exposing the enemy king often forces awkward defensive concessions. At the cost of the bishop-pair edge, Black accepts that White immediately has a rook, a bishop, and a knight against a queen and two pawns. The runner-up 15...Ne4 leaves White with a decisive advantage instead [pv:Ne4 Qe2 Nxc3 bxc3 Qe7].

16.Kxf2 gives Black a winning advantage (-2.25, Stockfish:16), and the continuation [pv:Kxf2 Ng4+ Kg3 Bxf3 Rg1] may leave White's pieces passive further on. Ke2 also gives Black a winning advantage; through [pv:Ke2 Bc5 Rf1 d5 Bd2] White would have kept the pieces actively placed—well-coordinated pieces are easier to defend with—but that line is clearly weaker, so Kxf2 remains the best try.

The most accurate move, maintaining Black's advantage (-2.12, Stockfish:16) through [pv:Ng4+ Kg3 Bxf3 Kxf3 Qh4], as the line may leave White's pieces passive—inactive pieces struggle to generate counterplay. In return, Black leaves a piece hanging immediately. Qe7 also leads to a clear advantage for Black but is clearly weaker via [pv:Qe7 h3 O-O-O Be3 d5], which could open the d-file for Black's rook in the line instead.

17.Kg3 gives Black a winning advantage (-2.08, Stockfish:16). After [pv:Kg3 Bxf3 Rg1 Nxh2 Ne4], Black may come out with a queen and three pawns for a rook and bishop—a surplus that usually outweighs the minor pieces. Ke2 was a comparable option that also gives Black a winning advantage via [pv:Ke2 Bxf3+ Kxf3 Qh4 Ne4], where White could have kept a rook and both bishops against a queen and two pawns while looking to target the knight on g4, but Kg3 is still the better try in a lost position.

The most accurate move, maintaining Black's advantage (-2.11, Stockfish:16) through [pv:Bxf3 Rg1 Nxh2 Ne4 d5]. In return, White's rooks are active on the open files, and the line may leave Black's pawn structure weaker with doubled, isolated, or backward pawns. Qf6 also leads to a clear advantage for Black via [pv:Qf6 Rg1 O-O-O Bd2 Bxf3], putting White's king under pressure and targeting the knight on c3, but Bxf3 is clearly the stronger continuation.

The most accurate move, 18...Qh4, maintains Black's advantage (-2.12, Stockfish:16) and is set to target the knight on e4 through [pv:Qh4 Ne4 O-O-O Be3 f5], at the cost of White's pieces becoming more actively placed in that line. By contrast, 18...f5 leads only to a slight advantage for Black via [pv:f5 h3 Qh4 Be3 Nxe3], preparing an immediate f-file break and potentially leaving White with a hanging piece, yet it lacks Qh4's direct challenge to the e4 knight.

Be4 makes matters worse, and Black now has a decisive advantage (-2.12 → -4.75, Stockfish:16). After [pv:Be4 f5 Bxf5 exf5 Ke2], Black keeps the upper hand;...f5 is the strongest continuation, maintaining that advantage through the forcing exchanges that follow. White missed the chance to play Ne4, which still gives Black a winning advantage [pv:Ne4 O-O-O Bd2 f5 Ng3].

19...f5 is the strongest continuation, maintaining Black's advantage (-4.56, Stockfish:16) through the forcing sequence [pv:f5 Bxf5 exf5 Ke2 Qf2+], heading toward a queen check that later keeps queen and two pawns for a rook and bishop—a lasting imbalance. 19...d5 is clearly weaker despite leaving a decisive advantage: [pv:d5 h3 f5 Bxf5 exf5], where White leaves a piece hanging as Black targets the bishop on e4.

The most accurate move, 20...Qf2+, keeps Black's queen and two pawns for a rook and bishop—a material imbalance that sustains long-term pressure—while letting the advantage shrink (-4.37, Stockfish:16) along [pv:Qf2+ Kd1 fxe4 Re1 d5]. A roughly comparable alternative was fxe4, which leaves Black with a decisive advantage by ending White's bishop-pair edge and creating a passed pawn on e4, [pv:fxe4 Nxe4 d5 cxd5 O-O-O], yet Qf2+ is the stronger way to continue that same material grip.

This move makes matters worse, and Black now has a decisive advantage (-4.37 → -6.06, Stockfish:16). After [pv:Kd3 fxe4+ Kxe4 Qg2+ Kd3], White's king is chased by...fxe4+ and...Qg2+, ending back on d3 while Black keeps the initiative in a forcing sequence that may eventually win on h1. White missed the materially better Kd1, which still leaves Black with a decisive advantage but keeps the king safer: [pv:Kd1 fxe4 h3 Qf3+ Kc2].

The strongest continuation is 21...fxe4+, which maintains Black's advantage and drives a forcing line: [pv:fxe4+ Kxe4 Qg2+ Kd3 Qxh1] (-5.82, Stockfish:16). By contrast, 21...d5 also leaves Black with a decisive advantage after [pv:d5 Bxf5 exf5 cxd5 Qf3+], but only once White leaves a piece hanging, and the line may eventually leave Black with a queen for a rook and a bishop—whereas fxe4+ is clearly the more accurate choice. Black went on to win.
